speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
That, notwithstanding any Standing Order, when the House adjourns on the day of adoption of this motion, it stand adjourned until a time and a day to be set by the call of the Chair,
That, during such adjournment, the provisions of Standing Order 28(3) respecting recall of the House shall continue to apply; and That, at any time during such adjournment, the Speaker may recall the House for the sole purpose of granting Royal Assent to any bill or bills, after which the House shall stand adjourned in accordance with this Order.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to participate in this debate, a debate which I think many members of the House have been looking forward to for some time.
I say that because this particular session has been a long one. It has been one of tremendous interest. Some of the issues we have discussed have probably been some of the most important issues that parliamentarians have had the opportunity to discuss and debate in many a year. In the last couple of years I have seen issues that have been very difficult, very divisive, and have created tremendous interest and debate across the country.
Yet, having said that, we have come now to this adjournment debate with good spirit in the House of
Commons. I am thinking of the debate that has occurred this last week. I would like to refer particularly to a column, in The Ottawa Sun today, by Douglas Fisher, where he talks about the debates that have occurred in this House over the past few days on the rule changes of Parliament.
He writes that this was not a debate for the so-called stars, this was a debate for the backbenchers. It was the backbenchers who very much led the way on this debate. It has been the backbenchers who expressed, often very eloquently, their dreams and aspirations for this institution, their concerns about how we as parliamentarians and this institution are viewed across the country.
Some of the interventions during this debate of the last few days have probably been some of the most interesting and thoughtful debates that I have seen in some time.
I want to come back to that in a few moments, but first I would like to give a thumbnail sketch of some of the bills that we have discussed in this particular Parliament.
Over the last couple of years, if my calculations are right, we have dealt with some 77 pieces of legislation from first and second reading, committee stage, report to third reading. We have dealt with a number of really important issues. It has been a very exciting parliamentary session.
I think back to the question of abortion, Bill C-43. It was an issue of great struggle for the members in this House. It was an issue of conscience which people on both sides of the issue have very strong feelings about. We saw the House struggle with that. We saw the issue passed in the House by a very close vote and then defeated in the Senate.
It is that kind of issue that, in many ways, has personified the type of Parliament and session that we all have had the "privilege" to participate in. It is that kind of issue that has forced us not to see ourselves purely as

April 12, 1991
Government Orders
partisans or as "participants in a sausage factory", a term that was used in the last few days debate.
We have been called, as parliamentarians, to look at some very difficult issues and determine where we individually stand, with the kind of perception and ideals we want to bring to our country. We have seen it in other debates. The question of Meech Lake was an issue this last couple of years.
Madam Speaker, you and I have very interesting perspectives, with you are a member from Quebec and I, a member from Alberta: one from the west and one from central Canada. We are faced with an issue that gets to the very core of our thoughts, ideas and dreams that we have for our country.
We saw the tremendous interest, the tension and the fascination that centred on that debate. Like you, Madam Speaker, I watched some of the meetings that were held on that issue. We can remember in particular the conference with the Prime Minister and the first ministers. We saw the dynamics that were alive there, and of course, saw its ultimate failure which has, once again, brought our country to a very important crossroads.
Maybe the last couple of years and some of the issues that we faced, discussed, thought about and struggled with have been a preparation for the debates that are going to occur in the near future.
The next issue we look at, as everyone knows, is going to be the whole question of the unity of our country, and the type of country that we want to pass on to our children and grandchildren. We heard the quip making the rounds: We now have new fathers and mothers of Confederation.
I think the last two years, as we have struggled with so many different issues, as we have tried to grasp such fundamental questions, have possibly prepared us for what is to come. There have been so many bills that we dealt with that pushed us, prodded us, and made us very conscious of our roles. I know that this preparation has been good for me personally. It forced me to think about my role as a parliamentarian, not as someone who is here to occasionally intervene in a debate or to rise from time to time and vote with my party, but, rather, I have been forced to examine my ideals, my dreams, my thoughts on so many different issues that have been before the House and before the country.
As a result of that I have been able examine myself as a parliamentarian and to prepare myself for what is coming over the next little while.
For me, one of the highlights of this whole Parliament is the one that I started talking about in the early part of my remarks, the rules package that we put before this House of Commons. I was a member of the McGrath task force, and before that the Lefebvre committee which dealt with the early stages of reform and I think set the stage or the groundwork for the McGrath task force.
I have had a particular interest in reform, and as Doug Fisher wrote in his column, I am one of those who have dreams and aspirations. I like the way he put it, and I hope I can find it in his column. He refers to members arriving in the House, and soon after developing an interest in the institution, developing some very strong attitudes about the kind of reforms that should be put in place. I was no exception to that. I was very fortunate to have been on the Lefebvre committee and then the McGrath committee. In both of those cases, we had an opportunity to look at this institution, to suggest often radical and very imaginative changes, and not only to suggest them, but to have an opportunity to spend time analyzing in detail the implications of those changes.
It was particularly interesting to go through that process, to see the McGrath task force complete its work in what is probably one of the best examples of members setting aside their partisan differences to work on a report they hoped would be adopted by the House of Commons.
In this debate on the largest reform package since McGrath, there were two speeches in particular that I want to refer to. I want to refer to the comments of the member for Surrey-White Rock-South Langley- which used to be Surrey-White Rock-Delta, and the speech given by the hon. member for Winnipeg Transco-na, which was originally Winnipeg-Birds Hill. I refer to those two particular members because they did something I could identify with, and that was very simple, they served with me on the McGrath task force.
They carried into this debate some of the same perspectives and concerns that I did and so I listened closely to them. I said to the hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona after his remarks that when listening to him I
April 12, 1991

had a flash of what I had hoped Parliament could become.
I saw an opportunity for us to have some real excitement. What I envisioned at that point was that we could enter into a dialogue, not where he might give a 20-minute speech and I might give a 20-minute speech and another member might give a 20-minute speech, but that we could actually stand here in this Chamber and discuss back and forth, point for point, our concerns, hopes and aspirations for a particular Standing Order and the implications it might have for this Chamber.
The closest we can come to that would be in committee of the whole. That is about as close as we can come in this institution to a really dynamic, one-on-one debate, that is short, not wrapped up in speech but in dialogue.
I saw that in his debate. I felt it could well have turned into a dialogue that I know the country would have liked to watch. The country would have been impressed to see that parliamentarians on opposite sides of the House with very different philosophical roots and very strong partisan differences could suddenly set aside those differences, philosophical or partisan, and say: "This is what I want for this institution".
The particular interest that the member for Winnipeg Transcona and I have is the whole area of committees because both of us very much supported that part of the McGrath task force and I think both of us believe that committees can be the real driving force of this institution.
We wanted to see and we still want to see committees having a strong influence on legislation, and also on policy. We dream of the day when committees will actually play a part in the drafting of legislation, by way of pre-study. The member for Winnipeg Transcona, I think, came to the House in 1979, a year before I was, and I know he has the same confidence that I have in members of Parliament.
We believe that if members of Parliament are given an opportunity to look at an issue, to talk to their constituents and to other Canadians, we are going to see some top quality laws and policy directions or guidelines for our country.
The hon. member for Winnipeg Transcona in his remarks looked very carefully at this particular package
Government Orders
that was before us as it related to committees. He quite rightly went through it with a very critical eye.
I told him after his remarks, or in fact I think it was before them, that when I sat down and did some of the initial drafting of committee reform, I had imagined him looking over my shoulder. If there was going to be one person who was going to be critical of that area, it would be the honourable member for Winnipeg Transcona. I knew he would look very carefully at the committees because he had a lot of confidence in what the McGrath task force had suggested. He had some concerns, but he did not want to in any way destroy the spirit of what had been established by that task force.
It was for me a fascinating experience to listen to his remarks. It renewed for me something that I needed to have renewed and that is a confidence in the people in this House and a confidence in this institution.
Now, at the end of the day, if we were to sit down and say: "Here are the issues, what do you agree on?", there may not be an awful lot. In some ways that is not as important as the fact that two members with such different approaches and positions can come together and look at an issue that is so important to us.
The other element that Doug Fisher mentioned in his column is in the headline: "It was a candid, sad debate". The sadness he refers to, and I have talked about the candidness he makes reference to being the quality of the speeches that were given on all sides of the House.
The sadness that Doug Fisher expresses is that the debate itself received so little media attention. This is understandable. The nature of the debate is technical and its scope narrow. It concerns, theoretically, only this House. But in fact, that is not the case. The rules under which we operate and the tone we set and establish in this place very much impact on the country, directly through legislation, but even more so indirectly, in terms of the flavour and tone of our debates and the perception that we send to the nation, whether it be through television or through reports of what goes on in this institution.
I agree with Doug Fisher. What we were faced with was a situation that really should have had the press gallery full. We should have had the people who cover this institution sitting up there, watching the heartfelt debate that was going on. If there is one thing that Canadians need to see, it is MPs at their best. Unfortunately, they so often see us at our worst, because 99 per

April 12, 1991
Government Orders
cent of what is covered in this institution is Question Period.
All members know that 90 per cent of Question Period or maybe more is show. It is the theatre. It is the place where we get up and take shots at each other, but few expect anything constructive to really come out of that hour. Yet, it is the entire focus of the Canadian public. The entire focus is on those 45 minutes of this House of Commons.
There is very little coverage of the work in committees. There is very little coverage of debates. There is precious little coverage of bills that pass through this place unanimously.
I have a regular experience in my riding when I go back and talk to my constituents and I, like other members, am criticized for our behaviour in the House. They may say to me: "Albert, we do not mean you, but the others". Well, the truth is that they mean me too. I am just as guilty as anybody else of tirades in the House, my hurled insults across the aisle. I am no saint. I am like everybody else.
People look at that and say: "Why do you not ever agree on anything". And I tell them that we do, regularly. There is probably not a week that goes by that we as a House do not agree unanimously on something. It may be to pass a bill at a particular stage or a motion. It may be to take an issue and refer it to a committee of this House for study. There are any number of things that we do unanimously. But of course because we do them unanimously, there is no tension, no confrontation. Therefore, there is no news.
I think it is really unfortunate, at a time when this country says to all of us: "We are looking for leadership".
I do not think by that they strictly mean the leaders of the parties. They want leadership from the hon. member for Edmonton, from me for Peace River, from Vancouver. They want leadership from individual MPs. They want us to be an example.
My point is that there is leadership in this House. It is not leadership restricted to a particular side of the aisle. There is leadership on all sides of this House. We saw that demonstrated in the debates of the last few days. We
saw members expressing themselves eloquently, passionately, and thoughtfully.
I think if Canadians are given an opportunity to see that, then their confidence in Parliament will increase. The confidence of Canadians in their individual members will rise and then we will be in a position to go into the all-important debate of the coming few months with some of the credibility that all of us need.
When Doug Fisher wrote his column, he wrote it as a person who watches Parliament, an individual who served in this House for a number of years, and since then has dedicated his life to watching and reporting it. His perspective as such I think has always been a little unique because he is someone who has been here. He knows the turmoils, the tensions, and the greatness of the institution. That is why his particular column reflects so well the reality that we are facing today.
We have come as parliamentarians through a couple of years of tremendous issues, tremendous tension, tremendous soul-searching and yet I think we end on a high note. We end on a note that is serious, thoughtful and demonstrates the kind of leadership that Canadians want to see.
I want to look in particular at a couple of the reforms in this package that did not get discussed a great deal. I want to look for a moment at the question of pairing. In the British House there has always been a system of pairing. In the Canadian House we had a system of pairing. It was informal but it was practised for years and years and years.
Then, I think it was shortly before I arrived in 1980, pairing broke down in the House of Commons. Those pairing relationships were destroyed. As a result, I think the House lost something very important. It was not so much that individual members can be paired, but it was an acknowledgement of the value and the importance of individual members.
How do you get that from pairing? I think it is this way. Let us take an issue or bill that I am particularly interested in, a bill that I may have worked on for years, that I may have been pushing through with all of the influence I have to make it a reality. Then, through some accident, through some quirk, I am unable to attend the
April 12, 1991

vote. I could be sick. I could be caught by a snow storm in my riding 4,000 miles from here. There are any number of reasons that I may not be able to be in this institution at the time of the vote.
If there is a system of pairing, an hon. member on the other side of the House would agree to cover for me. He or she would rise in the House and say: "The hon. member for Peace River was not here and I agreed to pair with him".
Therefore, I have an opportunity, even in my absence, to express my position on the bill. The hon. member in rising will say I would have voted with my party but, because I paired with the hon. member who would have voted for it. We would have put it back to where it would have been had we both been here.
The importance of that is that it gives credibility to members. It is a recognition that what we are doing in here has partisan implications, is often partisan driven, but nevertheless it is an acknowledgement that I, in my absence, am still important.
In this particular package we agreed to a new pairing process. I do not know how much it is going to be used. I have no idea if it is going to be used regularly or very infrequently. That is unimportant. What is important is that we once again acknowledge that individual members' votes are important. They have a right to have those expressions placed on the record. Even if they are prevented, for reasons of health or weather or whatever we face in this huge country that we live in, those expressions are still there.
I think what it does do is express a relationship. It is an expression of equality. It is an expression that we, on both sides of this House, attach a value to one another's participation, one another's voting, and one another's importance in the institution.
There was an article in the Ottawa Citizen on March 8, 1991, and it refers to the whole question that I have been talking about this morning, the question of credibility of the institution and of individual members.
The headline said: "Reforms may aid credibility." I just want to quote three paragraphs from this particular article, and this is not a personal reference:
In short, our elected leaders are making Parliament irrelevant.
Thus, it is difficult to understand all the opposition politicians'
Government Orders
complaints and moans about the common rules changes recently introduced by government House leader Harvie Andre. These reforms would do more to restore some credibility to the House and its occupants, than another roving committee of so-called great Canadians could.
In other words, this article is saying that the rules by which we govern ourselves are important. They do have an impact on how Canadians see us. We, as parliamentarians have been making Parliament irrelevant. I think it is unfortunate that is the kind of article that is written. Yet in fact, I think we would have to agree that it accurately reflects the feeling and attitude of a lot of our constituents.
We have to approach motions like these rule changes with sincerity and with honesty. We need to work together to make those reforms affect the House and the institution and our behaviour in a way that I think will help us re-establish our credibility.
We saw at the beginning of the debate some very strong statements about the rule changes. We saw very strong descriptive words being used, and yet in the end, after six days of debate, we saw a change in tone. Last night when we voted, and even before we voted, there were two things that happened which are significant.
Early yesterday afternoon, this House unanimously approved a House order that would allow us as a Parliament to adjourn today at 2 p.m.
We all agreed to that House order. It was passed through this House and as a result today we have a debate on the adjournment motion but we know at two o'clock that on division it is going to be passed.
I think that demonstrates what we as parliamentarians are trying to do together.
Second, there was a lot of controversy about what was going to happen to the votes. Yet if we look at what happened in the votes last night we find that parts of the package, particularly the Private Members' Business part, passed unanimously. I did not see that in any headlines this morning. It did not make a story. But in the midst of a fascinating debate and a fair amount of controversy we passed unanimously a part of the package, and we went further. We managed to work out among ourselves a voting pattern that would allow members to go home at about 1:15 in the morning.

April 12, 1991
Government Orders
Those are examples of co-operation that I think reflect well on the institution.
I say all that because we have been, in the last two years, through one of the most dramatic sessions of Parliament that we have seen in a long time. When we return on or about May 13, we are going to be into another very dynamic session of Parliament, but the dynamics of the next session are going to be even more important than the one we finished because in many ways what we will face will not be issues of great partisan import, but ones that will strike the very roots of our country.
When we enter into that debate, to a large extent all of us are going to be forced to examine the kind of country we want, the kind of co-operation that we can develop with people from other parts of the country than where we may live. We are going to be faced with an issue that will force us to examine our partisan differences very carefully. We are going to be forced to decide whether or not we as individual members are going to behave in a partisan way and score points off one another, or we are going to set aside those differences and try to build a consensus that will make Albertans feel comfortable in this country, make Quebecers feel comfortable in this country, or make maritimers feel comfortable in this country.
It will be a tremendous challenge for us because so often by habit or practice, we come into this House and immediately put on our partisan cloaks, get the fists up, and get ready to go at it. We are going to be forced to stop this because, if we do not stop, the price that the Canadian electorate is going to ask us to pay is more than our seats in the next election, whether or not we can survive that election. It is going to be much more than that. It is going to be Canadians saying to us, "why didn't you put the country ahead of your own personal ambitions?"
We are going to face a very difficult decision because, as we have been trained for years, we have by instinct trained and committed ourselves to behaviour that says we look first at the partisan opportunity and then, second, at the issue. Now I do not think that would be the case today. I think we are going to see that the issue we are going to face is an issue that we cannot afford to be deal with in such a way.
There are all sorts of rumours floating around as to what is going to happen in the next stage. I saw a report
on Canada AM this morning suggesting that Parliament will play a major role in this next constitutional stage of our country. I hope that report is true. I do not know that. I do not have any inside information that allows me to say that. I hope it is true, because I cannot think of one single institution or vehicle that we could use in the entire country of Canada that better provides the opportunity to bring all the perspectives of the nation together in one place, to participate in discussions about the country than this one.
I can remember when I was first elected in 1980, sitting back just on the other side of the Chamber in the seat over there in the back row, one of my first impressions was sitting there and, for the first time in my life, being surrounded by people who represented every part of Canada. People from the Northwest Territories, people from southern British Columbia, people from the mari-times, from Quebec, from Ontario and from all over the country. People who had perspectives that were so different from my own, who had experiences that shaped their thoughts and their approaches to Parliament and laws, and were so different from my own. This was not so much because of partisan differences, it was because their part of the country was very different from the part of the country that I lived in.
If that television report this morning was true, if we, as parliamentarians, have an opportunity to enter into debates on the constitutional future of our country, we are going to face one of the most exciting opportunities we have ever had, at least in my 11 years in Parliament. We can take almost any issue that might reflect on this country and bring to it a perspective that is unique, that expresses very clearly the distinctions that exist between different people and between different regions. We, as an institution, as a collective group, have probably the best opportunity to search out alternatives, to search out a consensus that we can offer up to the rest of the country.
I must say that is what I thought I was elected to do. When I had this dream as a young boy of becoming a member of Parliament, this is what I thought would happen. I was going to come to Parliament. I was going to think about the great issues of the day. I was going to struggle with them. I was going to do some real hard soul searching. I was going to be part of the process that drafted the laws that directed the land.
April 12, 1991

I received a big shock when I arrived at Parliament. I discovered, while I was sitting over there, that I had very little to do with legislation. Even as I talked to members who were on the other side of the House, at that time members of the government, they would say to me the same things that I felt.
They, too, felt that they were not part of the legislative process. That is why the McGrath task force was a turning point; that is why the question of committees is so important.
As we have gone through the three stages of reform we have had in the last 11 years-the Lefebvre committee, the McGrath task force, this set of rules that we have just put into the House of Commons, and the next one that is yet to come-

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order.
I wonder if the hon. member could explain how someone who has just moved to impose 10-minute speeches on everybody else, for all time, sees fit to go on for some 50 minutes now while others are waiting for an opportunity to speak. It seems a bit inconsistent.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I apologize to my friend for being so long but it is an opportunity I have not had in a long time-
Make it your swan song, Albert.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
-to express, with unlimited time, some of the thoughts that I have developed over my 11 years as a member of Parliament.
My friend says I am one of the people who has restricted other members to debate for 10 minutes. Now, he knows that is not true; he knows that, in fact, what we did in this rules change was to simply change the eight-hour rule to a five-hour rule, so that we have gone from 20 to 10. He will also know that in the McGrath task force it was the first time in my memory that we had suggested that speeches be shortened.
Government Orders
There is a consistency, and that is to give more members an opportunity to participate in the debate.
What I wanted to do this morning was take the few minutes that I have to lay out the type of session that we have just gone through. I wanted to talk about the rule changes and the way they impact on the institution. I wanted to tie that to the issues we are going to face in the next few weeks. The importance of the issues that we are going to face cannot be overestimated.
I think all of us know that we are going to have other issues, we are going to have other bills to debate in this Parliament. But the really important issue that we are all going to face is the question of national unity. I hope, and I want to express it even stronger than that, it is more than a hope, it is a strong desire, that Parliament be the focal point of that discussion.
I would like to be able to get up in the morning knowing that I am going to participate in a debate that is going to impact on the nature of this country, and more than to participate, to know that I am going to have an influence on it.
From what I can hear happening, that is what is going to happen. That is what is going to be the case, that we as members, are going to be able to participate in that debate in this House and we are going to have a chance to influence it.
I know, in terms of committees, that whatever this House addresses, whatever bill or motion we discuss, will probably at some point be referred to a committee of the House. Again, another opportunity for us as members to participate and to be part of the process.
I obviously have lots of papers in front of me and I could easily go on for another several minutes.
Oh, please do. Please do.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
I do not want to monopolize the time. That is not my intention. I did want to lay out these thoughts this morning, and to express to the House some of the concerns, attitudes and ideals that I would like to see us, as a House, express and live up to in the next little while.
I want to thank the hon. members for the opportunity to participate. Madam Speaker, I thank you for that chance. I want to say to all of the members that I hope they have a good rest over the recess. Most of us will be working in our ridings, but I hope we take the time to rest a little bit, because we are going to need to take the

April 12, 1991
time for solitude to think and to reflect. I hope all members do that.
I wish everybody a good recess, and I look forward to the debates and the excitement that is going to happen when we come back on May 13.

Madam Speaker, I would like to thank the parliamentary secretary for his grade 5 essay.
One should be a bit more generous and say grade 6 essay, and congratulate and give him high marks for his knowledge of geography, with high marks also for his self-congratulatory skills and in looking deeply and closely at a few trees. He saw a few trees. I do not know if he saw the forest.
One should give him high marks for delivering a 45-minute speech in the pursuit of bubbles, rumours and fantasies and for revealing the depth of the intellectual capacity of his government on whose behalf he has obviously spoken. Certainly, he deserves high marks for a masterful, political analysis of the situation today in Canada.
If that is what the cabinet of the Government of Canada can produce on the Adjournment Debate, then everybody understands why we are in trouble.
In reply, I would say that rarely in the history of Parliament has the government asked for an adjournment of Parliament immediately after returning from an Easter recess. I could hardly believe my ears when the parliamentary secretary wished us a happy recess and a good rest.
We have just come back from a recess. What is he talking about? Does he realize that we just had Easter and that we just got back from a recess?
Why are we having an adjournment? If there is a good reason, we would like to hear it. Canadians are entitled to hear it, but we did not hear it in the 50-minute speech of the parliamentary secretary.
To be quite fair in this debate, as we always try to be, I would add that Canadians would find nothing wrong with the government deciding to adjourn today and resume next week with a brand new session and a speech from the throne. Unfortunately, that is not the case.
At the same time, the country is in trouble because of high unemployment, dissatisfaction in Quebec and in the
west, understandable unrest amongst native people in Oka, James Bay, Alberta and British Columbia because of the lack of a federal role when it comes to proposed major construction of river dams in three provinces, and the dissatisfaction of the public with the way we manage our forests. subsubtopic: THE CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, if we are going to address all of Canadians' constitutional concerns, we will have to take a look at the Charter of Rights and Freedoms as well.
Many Canadians feel that the Charter is fine the way it is. But there are some who want to add to it the right to private property, or the right to medicare or the right to shelter. Others believe that the Charter should spell out our responsibilities and our obligations as well as our rights and freedoms. Still others want to eliminate the "notwithstanding clause". There are those who believe that Charter rights should apply only to Canadian citizens and not to refugee claimants or fugitives from foreign justice and others who want to delete references to official bilingualism or multiculturalism.
Whatever we do, we are bound to be unhappy at times when the Charter protects a right that some of us would rather it did not.

Madam Speaker, I rise today to call on the government to introduce legislation to support the use of ethanol and to ban MMT in Canadian automotive fuels.
April 12, 1991

We have heard this government on many occasions promise time and time again that it would set up a special program to encourage the use of grain alcohol as an octane booster for gasoline.
It took us six years to ban lead, and despite the government's so-called commitment to ethanol and the environmental impact, it allowed MMT, an insidious neurotoxic substance to replace lead in Canadian gasoline.
I am aware of several people who have worked in garages, car dealerships, muffler shops and gasoline bars, and one teacher who taught auto mechanics in a high school in Saskatchewan, who have serious neurological health problems. Two of these people have gone public. Some of our Canadian scientists have been calling and warning of these health effects for several years.
I have documents dated 1990 from medical schools and universities, as well as other institutions outlining in detail the truly horrible effects that allowing the continued use of this neurotoxin can have on the Canadian people.
This insidious substance accumulates in the bodies and the effects may not appear for several years. Because our children-

speechtext: Unfortunately, I must interrupt the hon. member. The hon. member for Delta.

Madam Speaker, I take this opportunity to remind members of the House and all Canadians that April is Cancer Month.
In Canada we estimate that over 100,000 new cancer cases will be diagnosed this year and that approximately
50,000	people will die of this disease.
The government is taking steps to change this. In collaboration with the provinces and the Canadian Cancer Society, the Department of National Health and Welfare is working to improve cervical and breast cancer screening programs in Canada. The department is also helping to fund the work of the Cancer 2000 task force "Strategies for Cancer Control in Canada".
I would like to applaud all those involved in the fight against cancer and their efforts toward reducing the burden of this disease on Canadians. I particularly pay tribute to the Canadian Cancer Society and the work it is doing.

Madam Speaker, it is another GST moment. Strange but true, case number two, the youth "tax credit caper".
If you are under 19 years of age and earn under $30,000, you do not qualify for a GST tax credit, even if you are a non-dependent. The only way the Conservative government will let you have the credit is if you have a child.
Today non-dependent Canadians under 19 can receive unemployment insurance; they can receive welfare; they can vote. But they do not get the same break under this regressive tax as other people do. It is a clear case of discrimination.
The Conservative government's hand is out for a large chunk of taxes from the often small pay cheques of youth, and will gladly accept GST to boot. But a tax credit? Forget it.
Stay tuned, the saga does continue. Coming up, the GST insurance.

Mr. Speaker, the Candlelighters Childhood Cancer Foundation of Canada is a national organization which represents 31 parent support groups from across Canada whose families have children with cancer. The difficulties these families face are enormous, given the emotional, psychological, financial and logistic problems that arise when a child suffers from cancer.
In providing the family support needed as treatments occur for their children, parents must often quit their jobs or take extensive leaves of absence. As presently regulated, these parents are not eligible for unemployment insurance unless they are diagnosed as suffering from extreme emotional distress. This approach has proven itself to be inadequate and potentially detrimental to an employee's career status.

April 12, 1991
As a result of this situation, Candlelighters has proposed a federal caretakers allowance through the unemployment insurance program which would provide benefits in the same manner as individuals receive benefits for maternity and quarantine leave. Many other nations already have such a program in place and a Canadian initiative in this regard would be a worthwhile, progressive step that would make the lives of many distressed Canadians slightly more bearable.
I have written to ministers on this and the answer I get is that it would set a-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member's time has expired.

Madam Speaker, I am sure that every member in this Chamber wishes that she or he could personally do something, anything, to help the Kurdish refugees before they die on the muddy mountainsides of Iraq and Turkey. Even hardened news reporters can be heard dissolving at scenes like the sight of a three-year old girl, barefoot, ankle deep in mud, wearing a thin little dress and shivering in the steady drizzle. Days, even hours, count with these children.
Canada must urge the involvement of the United Nations at the highest level, and fast. We must break the bureaucratic and political logjam, and cut through the complexities of agencies like the World Food Program, UNICEF and others. I am urging that a special representative of the Secretary-General or some United Nations emergency contingent oversee relief efforts immediately-
If only for the sake of these kids, we have to get the United Nations effectively and quickly involved. Above all, we have to get rid of that monstrous mass murderer, Saddam Hussein, to permit the relocation of the Kurdish people in their own homeland.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today to express my frustration
and dismay with the Government of Canada regarding the recent unemployment statistics which have been released for the Island of Cape Breton, part of which is my constituency.
The figures released by employment and immigration state there is 22.2 per cent unemployment, which is the official record, whereas in some of the communities it ranges between 40 and 50 per cent.
I have called upon the Government of Canada, and in particular the Minister of Employment and Immigration, as well as the minister responsible for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, to put in place programs which will address the very serious situation on the Island of Cape Breton.
I believe there is an obligation, both legal and moral on the part of the Government of Canada to attempt to do everything humanly possible to alleviate the fear, the frustration and the anguish of a people who have been singled out by the Government of Canada for such bad economic policy.

Madam Speaker, National Volunteer week is from April 21 to 27. During that week, communities in all regions of the country will pay tribute to their volunteers and use the opportunity to celebrate caring for others and compassion, which hold a fundamental place in the life of Canadians. With their generosity and dedication, volunteers contribute to the betterment of their fellow citizens and strengthen the whole fabric of society.
Despite that, the great importance of what they do is not yet recognized by all. To better understand the real contribution of volunteers, let us consider it in economic terms. If a monetary value were assigned to all the hours freely given by members of Canadian volunteer organizations, it would amount to approximately $13.2 billion a year. That is impressive to say the least.
Three cheers for Canada's volunteers!
April 12, 1991

Madam Speaker, Canada's cut and run logging of the past will become the exploit and sell out industry of the future unless action is taken immediately.
Canada's forest lands are being alienated, subdivided, sold off and urbanized by major forestry companies.
MacMillan Bloedel, the company which spends millions to lobby for clearcutting 3,000 hectares in both the Carmanah and Tsitika valleys, is now marketing 3,000 hectares of its Managed Forest Lands on Galiano Island in the Gulf Islands as an "investment in paradise".
This is profiteering and real estate speculation of forest lands on which they have received preferential tax assessment, paid no royalties or stumpage fees.
Forest lands must be managed for the public. Economic self-interest by multinationals cannot be allowed to destroy communities, jobs and the environment.
If Canada is indeed serious about protecting its forests and its international reputation, the respect for communities, for jobs and for the environment must be part of the business plan.
It is the responsibility of governments to ensure that message is delivered.

Madam Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to National Volunteer Week which is being held this year from April 21 to April 27.
This week, communities across the nation are paying tribute to those many Canadians who donate their time and energy to ensure the well-being of fellow citizens and to support the causes in which they believe.
Thirteen million Canadians, men and women of all ages, from all walks of life and from every cultural
background make volunteering an integral part of their lives.
Whether working on their own or through organized groups, they play a strong and vital role in ensuring that our society is more open and compassionate. Through their dedication and commitment, they help shape and strengthen our communities and are one of the most valuable natural resources this country has.
Volunteering fosters community spirit and promotes a sense of belonging. It connects individuals with their neighbours, with others sharing common interests or concerns and with Canadians nation-wide.
The strength of the volunteer spirit in Canada is a remarkable achievement. This nation truly owes a debt of gratitude to its many volunteers.

Madam Speaker, Louis Laberge's leaving the presidency of the Quebec Federation of Labour will be a dramatic occasion for all those who, during his 27 years at the helm of this dynamic union, got to know him and love him with his faults and good qualities.
But we already have the assurance that he will remain on the scene as full-time president of the Quebec Workers' Solidarity Fund, which he was so instrumental in creating in 1983 and has more than 100,000 shareholders and $350 million in assets. This fund is his pet project and he will certainly put his whole heart into running it well.
Nicknamed the grey eminence, but more affectionately known as our national "Ti-Louis", Mr. Laberge is an old friend. I was fortunate to know this bubbly, colourful personality in the 1950s when, with my father whom he called Dr. Hector, he sat on Montreal City Council. I was able to appreciate his energy, his fighting spirit and his dedication to all the causes he believes in.
Elected president of the QFL in 1964, the same year I was elected member of Parliament for Saint-Denis, Ti-Louis has become the likable but rough 67-year-old lion who will still make his presence felt in the labour

April 12, 1991
federation as president emeritus, although he says that he will leave the reins of power entirely to his successor and friend, Fernand D'Aoust, who opposed him for the presidency in 1964. I also have high regard for Mr. D'Aoust and I wish him an equally successful career at the head of an organization that is full of vitality.
I am pleased to wish Mr. Laberge and his wife, who has always supported him so well, all the best.
I am even more pleased that the new QFL headquarters will be in my riding of Saint-Denis, at the comer of Saint-Denis and Cremazie. This will bring me even closer to him. Long live Ti-Louis Laberge!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Unfortunately, I must interrupt the hon. member. The hon. member for Edmonton East has the floor.

Madam Speaker, Dr. James Plambeck of the University of Alberta's Chemistry Department has estimated that Mitsubishi's giant Al-Pac pulp mill on the Athabasca River will produce about 60,500 cubic metres of effluent every day.
Scores of thousands of people downstream from the mill draw their drinking water from that river. Who will guarantee all those thousands that they will suffer no ill effects from swallowing what has been estimated to be an average of a tablespoon of straight mill effluent every day?
As for the Minister of Environment, he will know that the scientific review panel report of the company's revised proposal has been thoroughly discredited as bad science.
Therefore, I call on the minister to exercise his undisputed authority to halt the mill's progress, at least until baseline studies are done on the Athabasca River system and other crucial conditions set in the original federal-provincial review have been met and completed unless he, too, is willing to drink a tablespoon of mill effluent every day.

Madam Speaker, the 26th Quebec Games finals will go down in history for the exceptional involvement of the entire population of the localities of Shawinigan, Grand-Mere and Shawi-nigan-Sud.
Under the skilfull direction of Mr. Michel Beliveau, president of the organizing committee of the 1991 Quebec Winter Games, at least 4,100 volunteers from the heart of the Saint-Maurice valley worked for 10 days to make this major sporting event a success.
I want to thank in particular the government of Canada, and the hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration, for its outstanding financial support.
My congratulations to all the people of the central part of the Saint-Maurice valley for this great success.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, today, as a matter of fact this afternoon, the government will be closing down this Parliament while 1.4 million Canadian men and women are out of work and 500,000 Canadians depend on food banks for their daily meals.
In Quebec, Madam Speaker, 5,000 businesses had to file for bankruptcy in 1990, and 14,000 cases of personal bankruptcy were reported. In Montreal, 223,000 people are jobless and the unemployment rate, which rose to 14 per cent, is the highest in the country.
In Quebec City, there are 24,000 people out of work; in Trois-Rivieres, 9,000, or 16 per cent of the population; in Sherbrooke, 8,000; in the Chicoutimi-Jonquiere area,
8,000	also. In the province, 335,000 people are on welfare and 3,000 others join them every month.
Major job losses are reported, Madam Speaker, at Air Canada, VTA Rail and CP and plant closures were decided by General Motors, Pratt and Whitney and Canadair just to name of few. Fourty-one thousand jobs were lost in the manufacturing sector in 1990. That is a disaster!
April 12, 1991

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Unfortunately, the hon. member's time is up.

Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Deputy Prime Minister. This government insists on closing down Parliament because it says it needs more time, more than a month, to write a new throne speech. This is a desperate attempt to put a fresh face on its tired and failed old policies.
Surely the government does not need another month to know that it has a very serious and crucial economic problem, and it is that there are more than 1.4 million people looking for work in this country.
Will the Deputy Prime Minister give us a commitment today that the new throne speech will contain an immediate program of full employment so that there will be at least a glimmer of hope for the more than 1.4 million Canadians who are out of work due to the discredited economic policies of this failed and tired old government.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am surprised at the context of the hon. member's question. It was my understanding that in the negotiations among House leaders, there was a genuine desire, after the passage of the resolution that would incorporate new rules in the House, there would be a period of time when we could get ready for the new session of Parliament.
It is quite normal to have more than one session in any Parliament. It has been the decision of the government to come forward with a Speech from the Throne which will reflect some of the concerns that affect the nation with regard to national unity, economic opportunities and the continuation of the good policies that have built a stronger Canada.
The hon. member will recognize that the figures this month indicate that for the first time in five months, there has been a net increase in total jobs created in this country. I think that is a positive sign.
Oral Questions
There should be no surprise about the fact that we were going to go through this bit of a downturn. It was clearly indicated in the budget speech presented by the Minister of Finance. We expect a turnaround to occur in the second half as the Minister of Finance predicted. In his seven years as Minister of Finance, his predictions have always come true to form.

Madam Speaker, the Deputy Prime Minister talks of a bit of a downturn. Why does he not admit, as the Minister of Finance was finally forced to admit, that we are in a desperate and serious recession caused by this government's economic policies.

Madam Speaker, the tragic situation workers find themselves in nation-wide does not seem to be taking a turn for the better.
In Trois-Rivieres, the unemployment rate is 16 per cent. That means 9,000 people out of work.
In Sherbrooke, there are 8,000 jobless people, and another 8,000 in the Chicoutimi area.
So, I would like to ask the acting Prime Minister this: Can he reassure the Canadian people and promise them today that the throne speech will contain full employment policies which will have an immediate impact?
Why does he not give a little hope to the Canadian people who are unemployed because of old and tired policies? Can he give us a positive answer today for the benefit of the jobless?

Madam Speaker, the old and tired policies are the policies that are advocated by the hon. member. They are policies which are throw-backs to the past which simply did not work when he was in government. We are not going to go back to that type of policy.
I remind him of the fact that under his policies back in the early 1980s, we had 14 per cent unemployment, we had 22 per cent interest rates and we had a disastrous recession in 1981-82.
What we have now is a set of policies that are designed to get us out of the recession that we are in today. They are designed to get interest rates down. We are seeing some signs of recovery in that. I need only remind the hon. member of what has happened in the housing

April 12, 1991
Oral Questions
market. We are seeing a substantial increase in housing sales from a level of about 2,500 to a level of close to
6,000	from January to February.
I quote from Mr. John Winter, who is a leading retail analyst in Toronto. He says: "I think March will be better than February and, quite frankly, I think we have seen the bottom of this slump." This is consistent with what we have been saying as a government. It is consistent with what the Royal Bank and what the Conference Board have been saying.
If the hon. member would quit walking around with a little cloud over his head, only talking doom and gloom, he might be able to see that as well.

Madam Speaker, I do not know why this minister is revelling in the problems caused for millions of Canadians due to the policies of his own government for which he was taking credit.
Why is the minister continuing to rely on the same policies to get us out of the recession that he admits got us into the recession? If the minister will not give us a commitment today for new policies of full employment, I ask him to tell us what his government is doing right now for the more than 1.4 million Canadians who are standing in the unemployment lines all across this country. Give us an answer right now. Give Canadians some hope.

Madam Speaker, I do not know what the hon. member is thinking about when he says I am revelling in the difficulties that Canadians are having. I am not revelling at all. I do not like it at all. What I do know is that the policy prescriptions that we are following are the right ones to get us out of the recession that we are in today.
We saw, from 1984 right through to the spring of 1990, where those policies brought us record growth, that Canada was number two, only after Japan, of the major industrialized countries. There were 1.6 million jobs created in that period of time. So these policies are working.
I say to the hon. member, if he has any ideas, if he has any alternative policies, let us know and let us have them, but I have yet, in the six and a half years that I
have been Minister of Finance, heard anything from the Liberal Opposition as to what alternative policies it has. Canadians are looking for more than just straight negative opposition, what they are looking for is a positive policy approach.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
In Atlantic Canada, unemployment insurance recipients are experiencing extraordinary delays in having their UI claims processed; in many cases, from 10 days to 2 weeks. This is devastating in an area where unemployment is running over 20 per cent. For those people whose only source of livelihood is their UIC cheque, it is totally unacceptable, even tragic.
I would ask the minister to explain why this is happening and what is being done to rectify it.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I sympathize with the hon. member's question and its intent because we have had some processing problems in some of our offices. What we have been trying to do as a result is do more through the mail and more on the telephone, and we have improved our claims processing. We are putting more people in our offices to ensure that we can speed up the processes for getting cheques to people as rapidly as possible.
Sometimes it comes as well from people coming in to us with incorrect information which delays the process and takes up some of our personnel time. But we are doing the best we can to ensure that the backlogs come down, and they are being reduced very quickly.

Madam Speaker, whatever the reason for this delay, there is hope that we are witnessing a temporary interruption and that this greatly reduced level of service is not something that can be expected on a long-term basis. That is the concern. So I would ask the minister to undertake to assure this House that her department will not accept a degradation of service for UI claimants as a regular occurrence.
April 12, 1991

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, far from it being a regular occurrence, the service throughout our department has improved quite considerably over the last two or three years. I answered the first question dealing with the difficulties that the hon. member pointed out and I am quite prepared to accept that, but over time we have improved the service. Not only that, the programs we have put in place are programs that enable people to get back to work faster and to get trained for other jobs. Even in the Atlantic region which the hon. member represents, where I recognize there are particular difficulties, there is a mismatch between the training that people have and the jobs that are available because there are some jobs available. I would point out that in the month of March across Canada, there were 2,000 more jobs than there were the month before. There was an increase in the unemployment rate because of more people coming into the labour force.
To reinforce what my colleague said about the economy turning around, we are seeing more jobs being created and there were more created last month.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. Aerospatiale, which is part of the consortium that is going to purchase de Havilland, already had its president as its official lobbyist in Canada. On April 5 Fred Doucet became an official registered lobbyist for Aerospatiale.
Could the Deputy Prime Minister tell us what possible advantage Aerospatiale could expect to gain by having a former fundraiser for the Prime Minister, a former chief of staff, and in fact a man who got married at 24 Sussex Drive, as its official lobbyist?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Madam Speaker, that question would be more appropriately addressed to Aerospatiale. He can certainly phone them up and ask them. I think that would give him the best answer.

Madam Speaker, we are in a nation where there is a great deal of distrust and questioning about the political process. The
Oral Questions
whole country is, and the Deputy Prime Minister knows that.
I think they would be wondering whether there is more concern about producing jobs for the Prime Minister's cronies than the 26,000 people who are going to be affected by this purchase.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sure the hon. member has a direct question to pose to one of the ministers.

Yes, Madam Speaker. Is the Deputy Prime Minister aware of whether or not this close friend of the Prime Minister has in fact approached the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology, or the Prime Minister, to discuss with him how they are going to preserve those 26,000 jobs that are likely to be affected by the de Havilland purchase, or is it in fact more important to see that the former Conservative cronies get jobs?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I really cannot add any more to the obvious answer provided by the Deputy Prime Minister, and that is to phone those who signed the contract, but I say to the hon. member that when the Prime Minister came into office he said he would bring in a lobbyist registration act. That has come into effect and is in force. It is that information that is now public and I would suggest that the hon. member work on the basis of that type of knowledge rather than the kind of innuendo which he is so capable of throwing around here.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
It has been seven years now that this government has promised improvements to the Bankruptcy Act of Canada. God knows, we have waited for decades of successive Liberal governments to bring in appropriate changes to the Bankruptcy Act of this country that would give a measure of justice to those workers who have lost their jobs and to those suppliers who have not been paid as a result of bankruptcies.
Yesterday, after six months in office-

April 12, 1991
Oral Questions

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Normally, the first questions asked by the New Democratic Party would have the possibility of one question and two supplementaries.
I am really trying very hard to see the connection between the first question asked and the one being asked by the member now. Maybe he would want to rephrase his question and put it now.

Madam Speaker, my hon. colleague for Windsor-St. Clair pointed out that there is a danger of
26,000	jobs being lost in de Havilland.
My question deals with job losses.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Then the hon. member will put his question now.

I understand why they are so sensitive about this on both sides.
Can this government tell the people of Canada in what month, in what year and in what decade can we expect to get the changes to the Bankruptcy Act that will provide justice to workers who have lost their jobs as a result of bankruptcies?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the government does share the concern expressed by the hon. member.
I can assure him that it is a matter that is under very active consideration. I hope that in the not too distant future we will be able to respond to the very valid point that the hon. member made. I just ask him to be patient a little longer.

Madam Speaker, my question today is for the Minister of Justice.
Recently, there was a very significant court case in British Columbia. The Gitksan-Wet'suwet'en people, we understand, are going to take this to appeal. Eventually, it will end up in the Supreme Court.
There is a large number of people in British Columbia and in other parts of Canada who feel that it would save a lot of time and money if this appeal was directly referred to the Supreme Court.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member will put his question now.

Madam Speaker, my question is to the justice minister.
Can this case not be referred directly to the Supreme Court, rather than going through the various appeal processes which will involve a lot of funding and a lot of time, which is unnecessary at this time?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, technically and theoretically it is possible to refer questions to the Supreme Court of Canada.
We have not had a formal request to do so. We are undergoing discussions with parties to the case. We are no longer party to the case since the claim against us was dismissed.
I would point out, though, that it is unusual to refer a matter as factually complex as this to the Supreme Court of Canada. I think all the parties would want to consider what was the best way to clarify the issues. It is a case of very complex fact in law.
Our disposition is to be as co-operative as possible. We are having informal discussions, but as yet have had no formal request from any of the parties.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister, and it is with regard to the proposed sale of de Havilland.
It has been confirmed this morning in writing by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Mr. Fred Doucet, the former chief of staff and friend of the Prime Minister, has been hired as the chief lobbyist to lobby both the government and Investment Canada on behalf of the consortium of Aerospatiale and Alenia.
Given that the government thus far has failed to stand up for the Canadian aerospace industry or provide any details whatsoever of the proposed deal, how can Canadians now have any assurance whatsoever that the interest of the workers at de Havilland, our aerospace industry and research and development will take precedence over the interest of a former chief of staff and long time personal friend of the Prime Minister?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
The people of Canada can have trust and confidence that this will bring net benefit to Canada because the previous arrangement brought tremendous net benefit to Canada. They have moved from 2,800 jobs
April 12, 1991

in 1974 to a level way beyond that. They have developed a strong order book. They have got a good distribution network. This was all done when Boeing took over.
As we move to a different purchaser, we will ensure that net benefit to Canada is there again.

Madam Speaker, the question is, as the minister put it, a question of trust.
I return to the Acting Prime Minister and ask him very simply, will the allegiance of the government lie with the workers of de Havilland and the aerospace industry, or will the allegiance of the government lie with a former chief of staff and long time personal friend of the Prime Minister? Whose side will the government be on? Let us have some confidence and trust for a change on behalf of Canadians.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. minister may want to answer, but it is very difficult for the Chair to accept that this is a question regarding the administration of government. The decision was made by a private company and not by the government. I do not see how it is a question regarding the administration of the government.
The hon. minister may want to answer. If not, I cannot allow the question.
I have heard the comment made by the hon. member for York West and I do not think he meant to imply any impropriety from the Speaker. I am sure that he will want to rise right away and withdraw the comment.
I concur with your sentiments and I think you are absolutely right.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is also to the Deputy Prime Minister.
It concerns Telesat Canada. In 1985, the Prime Minister laid down the law: No government-owned corporation could hire lobbyists to lobby cabinet. Now we hear that Telesat Canada, the government-owned satellite company, is paying the Prime Minister's former assistant, Bill Fox, and a recent Conservative Party president, Bill Jarvis, to lobby cabinet and to overrule a CRTC decision.
Oral Questions
Will the Deputy Prime Minister now stand in his place and respect the rules laid down by the Prime Minister and put an end to this abusive process?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the government does not own the company. We are a shareholder, we have an interest in the company, but it is a private company.
Whatever they do is their business. It is Telesat's business. The government will act in its own best interest and in the interest of the nation.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
The majority shareholder in this corporation is the Government of Canada, and therefore it is a government corporation.
I want to ask a supplementary. First of all, cabinet itself could be in a very difficult position. By overruling the CRTC it increases the value of Telesat. Then it will privatize it. At the same time, of course, Tory friends will be rewarded by doing the lobbying.
I want to know this time whose side the Prime Minister is going to be on. Is it the side of the Tory lobbyists or on the side of the people of Canada, for a change?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Telesat hired communications consultants to help them prepare their case. I know they did hire them because they happen to be good.
Now, they will do what they feel is appropriate and the government will do what we have to do in the best interests of the nation.

Madam Speaker, my question is to the Deputy Prime Minister.
Another Canadian manufacturer has just been deep-sixed by free trade. Wolverine Copper Tubing of Annacis Island, British Columbia, has suddenly and in the middle of contract negotiations closed its doors and is moving production south of the border, throwing 180 British Columbians out on the street. Wolverine is an Alabama

April 12, 1991
Oral Questions
based, U.S. company that is, I might add, the sole manufacturer of copper tubing in Canada.
What actions, if any, has the government taken to forestall this closure and to protect the Canadian jobs that are at stake? If the minister has not taken any actions, what actions is he prepared to take?
Finally, why was Investment Canada allowed to sell out our Canadian manufacturing industry to foreign interests, when this is the obvious result?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think the hon. member should know that there is a similar Wolverine operation in my home riding of London, Ontario, and it makes the same products. I do not know what he is talking about when he says that the sole supplier has disappeared.
Get your facts right.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: More important is the effect of the free trade agreement. If the hon. member will look at the increase in manufacturing jobs in British Columbia in 1988, 1989 and 1990 in anticipation of the trade agreement, the net benefit is on a huge positive side, not a negative side.

Madam Speaker, Wolverine owns three plants. I say there is one down and two to go.
John Quarles, President and CEO of Wolverine in Alabama, has cited economic reasons for the closure. In a recent telephone conversation he said: "We are fighting those high Canadian interest rates and the GST, and we just can't make a go of it".
Will the minister not admit that this government's tragic monetary policy, its high interest policy and its over-valued Canadian dollar, combined with the GST, are killing our manufacturing industry and mothballing our economy?
Will he also not admit that the impact of these measures, when we combine them with the free trade agreement, is encouraging a virtual exodus of manufacturers out of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I certainly will not admit such a thing. As a matter of fact the exact opposite is the case.
Right on.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
The old manufacturers' sales tax which built in a cost of operation 4 per cent or 5 per cent more than Canadian operations should ever have to carry has been totally removed. What has happened is that the Canadian manufacturing establishment has benefited to the tune of 3, 4 or 5 per cent with the removal of the old federal sales tax.
In terms of the free trade agreement, we have put in place accelerated tariff reductions in a number of areas to benefit industries similar to that and a number of manufacturing industries in British Columbia, all to show that the manufacturing sector in many cases wants an acceleration of this agreement and nothing other than that.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Revenue.
The minister will know, if he has examined the figures, that one-day shopping trips to the U.S. over the past two or three weekends show that the volume has reached alarming proportions. I would like to ask the minister about the new policy, which I understand is currently being drafted by cabinet to address these concerns.
What is the thrust of this new policy likely to be? When is the new policy likely to be announced?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member touches on a very serious problem that affects not only the federal government but, more important, the provincial and municipal governments, the private sector and labour itself.
From a Customs standpoint, the hon. member will know that we have moved ahead in accelerating the use of technology, adjusting work forces to conform to demands and putting in a pilot project to make a more efficient and effective way of collecting taxes and duties. That is on the Customs side.
April 12, 1991

On a broader side, the government is working toward creating and taking the leadership in creating a program that will bring in the private sector, that will bring in labour, that will bring in the provinces and that will bring in the municipalities so that we can deal with this on a society-wide basis and make sure that we come up with a resolution that will resolve this matter sooner, rather than later.

With reference to the reply I got, Madam Speaker, I want to remind the minister that facilitating the entry of Americans into Canada at border points is a good idea. We agree with that, but that is only one issue.
Addressing the attraction to shop in the U.S. on a regular basis by Canadians is a very different issue.
My supplementary question is for the same minister. With an estimated annual $1 billion in lost retail sales in Ontario alone for the current year, not to mention the thousands of lost jobs in the retail industry, can the minister tell me what concrete and immediate plans he has to address this tendency for more and more Canadians to do their regular weekly shopping in the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I touched on that question in my first response but, to be more specific about it, as far as the customs operations are concerned I repeat that we are accelerating the use of technology through automated cash registers to make way for a more efficient and effective way of collecting duties and taxes.
We have put in recently in British Columbia a pilot project which is going to relieve the congestion at the border, revitalize the tourist industry in British Columbia, and allow for expanded commercial traffic in that province. We are going to be monitoring that and hopefully be expanding it to other parts of the country.
I have finished meeting on a bilateral basis with mayors from border communities this last week. We look forward to continuing to meet with them to come up with a marketing program that will allow Canadians to realize that by going south of the border to shop they in fact are hurting themselves, Canadian retailers and the Canadian economy as a whole.

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Agriculture.
Farmers in western Canada have a deadline that is rapidly approaching. They must decide whether to sign
up for GRIP, for revenue insurance, for crop insurance, or in fact for nothing at all. An important part of that decision is whether or not deficiency payments will be tied to any or all of these programs.
Will the minister tell Canadian producers today whether or not they must sign up for any of these programs in order to be eligible for deficiency payments?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Agriculture; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I am sure the hon. member knows-and I would appreciate if he would convey this to his producers-we did establish a set of principles that were agreed to by the provinces which would govern us in the development of a third line of defence package.
Largely, the principles reflect the multifaceted nature of the problem and the fact that it would be in everyone's best interest to get as many people as possible into the long-term safety net process. That is important from the standpoint of the producers, as well as the provinces, and particularly those who have yet to commit fully to the Net Income Stabilization Account, which is very key and vital to the long-term stability of the agricultural community.
One of the principles is that to the extent possible any transitional assistance should be tied to the long-term safety net program and delivered to that program if possible. It is within the spirit of those principles that we are attempting to develop that plan.

Madam Speaker, the government says that GRIP is voluntary. If it is voluntary then deficiency payments should not be tied to it. If the payments are tied to GRIP then the government should have the decency at least to let producers know that.
I ask the minister again, very simply, are deficiency payments tied to GRIP or are they not tied to GRIP? Farmers have a right to know so that they can make a proper decision based on market matters as opposed to what this government is doing with respect to programs.

April 12, 1991
